notes: This models EXTERNAL adjacent-role entry points into cybersecurity, not lateral moves within cybersecurity (e.g., a Defensive Cybersecurity analyst moving into a dedicated Purple Team function is a real and common path, but it's an internal move between existing Work Roles, not an adjacent-role transition -- it doesn't belong in this dataset).

Step 3 (tagging each feeder role with baseline Skill/Knowledge IDs it typically already has, so 'skill gap to close' can be computed automatically against a target Work Role's requirements) is deliberately deferred as a fast-follow -- this file gives the pathway list needed for the visualization now.

Color-wheel cross-check: these 18 feeder pathways land overwhelmingly in Yellow, Green, Blue, and White target roles. Red is reached only through the CTF/hobbyist non-job pathway, and Purple isn't reached by any external feeder at all -- both are consistent with real industry hiring patterns (red-team hiring pipelines don't rely on adjacent corporate job titles the way blue/build/govern roles do), and reinforce that Purple in particular is structurally an intra-cyber move, not an adjacent-role one.

No single feeder role cleanly produces a 'Range Engineer' (infra + blue tooling + red simulation) -- the closest combination is Systems Administrator or Network Engineer plus hands-on blue/red exposure gained on the job. This supports treating Cyber Range Engineer/Operator as a candidate new Work Role (or an explicitly multi-role job title) in the scope-gap analysis, rather than expecting an adjacent-role pathway to explain it.

7 of 44 Work Roles aren't reached by any external feeder pathway: Cybersecurity Workforce Management, Executive Cybersecurity Leadership, Product Support Management, Systems Authorization, Technology Portfolio Management, Enterprise Architecture, and Database Administration. This looks like a real pattern rather than a gap to fill: these are typically filled by internal promotion from within cybersecurity or a closely adjacent IT specialty, not by a lateral hire from an unrelated field. Worth deciding whether the visualization should represent that explicitly (e.g., 'internal progression only') rather than leaving it looking like an oversight.

feeder_roles.typical_background: Proficient in one or more programming languages, software design and testing practices, version control, and the general software development lifecycle. Typically lacks formal security-specific training.

targets.rationale: Nearly identical day-to-day work, with security requirements and threat modeling layered on top of existing development skills.
Especially relevant for engineers already working with ML pipelines; requires learning adversarial ML concepts and security-specific evaluation techniques.
Same skillset applied to systems rather than application code.
Strong engineering fundamentals transfer directly into applied security research.

feeder_roles.typical_background: Comfortable with CI/CD pipelines, infrastructure-as-code, cloud platforms, containerization, and automation scripting.

targets.rationale: Automation and systems fluency transfers directly; mainly needs security-specific monitoring and analysis knowledge.
Very close overlap -- DevOps already operates and hardens the infrastructure this role secures.
Natural fit for practitioners already building monitoring/alerting pipelines; requires learning compliance frameworks on top.

feeder_roles.typical_background: Deep familiarity with OS administration, patching, user/account management, backup and recovery, and enterprise IT operations.

targets.rationale: Direct extension of existing systems knowledge into a security-analysis lens.
Deep systems knowledge is directly useful for understanding what's normal vs. compromised during response.

feeder_roles.typical_background: Deep knowledge of routing/switching, network protocols, firewalls, and network architecture.

targets.rationale: Directly builds on existing network infrastructure expertise.
Network visibility is central to defensive monitoring; requires learning detection/analysis tooling.
Deep protocol knowledge is a strong foundation for finding network-level weaknesses.

feeder_roles.typical_background: Structured testing methodology, test-case design, defect tracking, and often some scripting/automation.

targets.rationale: Testing discipline transfers well; requires learning vulnerability classes and adversarial thinking.

feeder_roles.typical_background: Deep database platform knowledge, query optimization, backup/recovery, and access control within database systems.

targets.rationale: Database-specific expertise becomes one input into broader systems security analysis.
Data classification and access-control fluency is directly relevant to technical privacy work.

feeder_roles.typical_background: Statistical analysis, data wrangling, visualization, and often scripting in Python/R/SQL.

targets.rationale: Analytical rigor transfers well; requires learning threat-intelligence tradecraft and adversary frameworks.
Especially strong fit for data scientists already familiar with ML model development and evaluation.

feeder_roles.typical_background: Broad, shallow exposure to many systems, strong troubleshooting and customer-facing skills -- often the single most common entry point into IT generally.

targets.rationale: The single most common real-world on-ramp into a SOC analyst role; requires substantial new security training, but the troubleshooting mindset transfers well.
Broad exposure to how systems normally behave is a real asset in spotting what's abnormal during an incident.

feeder_roles.typical_background: Scheduling, stakeholder management, budget tracking, and risk registers -- typically without technical security depth.

targets.rationale: Same core PM discipline, applied to security-relevant projects.

feeder_roles.typical_background: Formal audit methodology, regulatory framework fluency (SOX, HIPAA, etc.), and evidence-gathering/reporting discipline.

targets.rationale: Audit methodology transfers directly; requires learning IT/security-specific control frameworks.
Regulatory fluency transfers well, especially from healthcare (HIPAA) or finance (GLBA) backgrounds.

feeder_roles.typical_background: Legal research, regulatory analysis, contract review, and formal writing.

targets.rationale: Strong fit for attorneys with a privacy-law background specifically.

feeder_roles.typical_background: Investigative procedure, evidence handling and chain-of-custody discipline, and structured report writing.

targets.rationale: Chain-of-custody rigor is directly relevant; requires learning digital forensics tooling.
Investigative background is a strong foundation for insider-threat casework.

feeder_roles.typical_background: Structured analytic techniques, threat-actor assessment, all-source analysis, and briefing/reporting to leadership. Note: much of this background is exactly the intelligence-cycle content we deliberately excluded from the general-industry graph (Section 4-6 of the fork decision log) because it doesn't translate for most practitioners -- but it's precisely what makes this population unusually well-prepared for these two targets specifically.

targets.rationale: Threat-actor assessment tradecraft transfers almost directly; mainly needs cyber-specific technical depth.
Structured analytic techniques transfer directly to insider-risk casework.

feeder_roles.typical_background: Instructional design, curriculum development, and adult-learning facilitation.

targets.rationale: Directly applies existing instructional-design skills to cybersecurity content.
Directly applies existing training-delivery skills; needs cybersecurity subject-matter depth.

feeder_roles.typical_background: Clear technical documentation, information architecture, and working with subject-matter experts to translate complexity into readable material.

targets.rationale: Documentation skills transfer well to curriculum content; needs cybersecurity subject-matter depth.

feeder_roles.typical_background: Risk quantification, business impact analysis, and reporting to leadership and boards.

targets.rationale: Risk-analysis discipline transfers directly; needs cybersecurity-specific threat and control knowledge.
Business risk-quantification skills transfer directly to vendor/supply-chain risk.

feeder_roles.typical_background: Broad product knowledge across many security tools, strong communication skills, and comfort presenting technical concepts to varied audiences.

targets.rationale: Broad exposure to many vendors' architectures is a real head start, though hands-on design depth still needs to be built.

feeder_roles.feeder_title: CTF Player / Self-Taught Hobbyist (not a prior job -- a prior practice)
feeder_roles.typical_background: Hands-on exploitation practice via Capture-the-Flag competitions, home labs, bug bounty participation, or independently-pursued certifications (e.g. OSCP), often without any formal cybersecurity job history yet.

targets.rationale: This is the dominant real-world on-ramp into red-team roles -- more so than any adjacent job title. Worth modeling explicitly since it's a prior *practice*, not a prior job.
Hands-on exploitation experience transfers directly to structured vulnerability assessment work.

feeder_roles.typical_background: Deep knowledge of industrial control systems (ICS/SCADA), PLCs, plant/process engineering, and physical safety and reliability requirements -- typically from an electrical or controls engineering background rather than traditional IT.

targets.rationale: This is the single most natural feeder into OT security -- deep plant/process knowledge is the hard-to-teach part; cybersecurity concepts layer on top.
Physical infrastructure fluency transfers, but requires substantial new IT/network security depth.
